lines.text: Red dunes, ancient rock art and a hard road to freedom. This is the story of Namibia, from the oldest desert on Earth to independence.
Some fifty-five million years ago the Namib Desert began to form, a coast of towering red dunes, often called the oldest desert in the world.
About thirty thousand years ago, people in a cave now called Apollo 11 painted stones, some of the oldest art in Africa.
Much later, San hunters carved thousands of animals into the rocks of Twyfelfontein.
In 1884 Germany seized the land as the colony of German South West Africa.
Windhoek grew up in the highlands at its centre, and became the capital.
From 1904 German troops killed most of the Herero people and half the Nama, the first genocide of the twentieth century.
In the desert, diamonds built the town of Kolmanskop. When the miners left, the sand moved in, and drifts through its empty houses still.
Sam Nujoma would lead the long fight for independence, and become the nation's founding president.
Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, born in 1952, would become Namibia's first woman president in 2025.
By then South Africa ruled the land and had brought apartheid. In 1960 SWAPO was formed to fight for freedom.
From 1966 SWAPO and South Africa fought a long border war that lasted almost a quarter of a century.
And in 1990 Namibia was free at last, an independent country on the edge of the Namib.
From painted stones to a free nation, Namibia's story is one of endurance.
